<reason>Side A (CON) delivered the flashier case — the engineer/wind analogy, the Rebuttal 2 concession-trap quoting B's own brakes back as "my thesis in their vocabulary," and the closing "redundant or fatal" dilemma. But Side B (PRO) built the more durable route to victory. B's approval-vs-sufficient-cooperation distinction, set up in Rebuttal 2 and driven home in the closing, dissolved A's dilemma: a community can formally object while still cooperating enough to make restoration work, and B assesses feasibility (funding uptake, participation, monitoring) before release, so the override clause does real work A's consent rule would block. A's counter — grudging cooperation is "consent wearing a frown" — redefined consent behaviorally, colliding with A's own justice and "consultation is theater" arguments. B also answered both pressure questions with concrete brakes (livelihood floor, cancel/pause conditions), while B's Q1 exposed the individual-holdout/community-veto tension in A's logic. A won on style; B won the central analytical clash on the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 trap — arguing B's conceded brakes (pause if unviable, cancel if livelihoods unprotectable, "sufficient cooperation") amount to CON's thesis with worse sequencing — was the debate's most damaging single move. B's closing decisively pre-answered it: "This is not a difference in sequencing: more consultation does not guarantee agreement," plus the approval/cooperation split, neutralizing A's strongest play just before A's closing deployed it.</best_rebuttal>
